hook.text: Every pipeline ends by writing data somewhere. Here are a million sales, made up for this video, written twice. As a CSV file, they take thirty-nine point two megabytes. As Parquet, a columnar file format, nine point four.

hook-read.text: Ask both for revenue by category. DuckDB reads every byte of the CSV, and five megabytes of the Parquet file. Same rows, same answer: only the layout differs.

plan.text: Layout is what the warehousing round asks about: nine questions, from rows and columns to formats, partitions, cost and where it all lives. Seven get measured on these same rows.

rows.text: Question one. What is OLTP versus OLAP, and how does storage differ?

rows-oltp.text: OLTP, online transaction processing, runs the application: many small reads and writes, one order at a time. So it stores each row's fields together: one order, one place.

rows-olap.text: OLAP, online analytical processing, runs the reports: a few columns across millions of rows. So it stores each column together: every sale ID, then every date, and so on.

cols.text: Question two. Why is columnar storage faster for analytics? A query reads only the columns it names. The page's query names three of six: category, units and amount.

cols-read.text: That's why DuckDB read only five of the Parquet file's nine point four megabytes. A row format mixes those three fields in with all the rest, so the CSV was read whole.

cols-more.text: Values of one type, side by side, also compress well and run in batches.

fmt.text: Question three. Compare Parquet, ORC, and Avro.

fmt-columnar.text: Parquet and ORC, optimized row columnar, are both columnar and compressed, with per-column statistics that let a reader skip data. Parquet is the default nearly every engine reads; ORC grew up around Hive, in the Hadoop world.

fmt-avro.text: Avro, a row-based binary format, writes whole records, and its files carry the schema they were written with. It suits streaming, one record at a time, often on Kafka, a distributed log, and its compatibility rules let a schema evolve.

fmt-csv.text: And over CSV, Parquet carries types and a schema, and here it's under a quarter of the size. Columnar for analytics, Avro for records in motion.

cmp.text: Question four. Why is compression more effective in columnar formats? A column holds one type, often with few distinct values.

cmp-region.text: Region has four. Parquet writes each one once, in a dictionary, then about three bits a row: a million regions in three hundred eighty kilobytes, against five and a half megabytes of text.

cmp-amount.text: Amount is random to the cent, so it only shrinks from six point eight megabytes to four point two.

cmp-sort.text: Sorting before writing makes long runs. In date order, a million dates take three kilobytes. Sorted by region, the region column falls to five hundred fifty-four bytes.

cmp-codec.text: Codecs trade too. Zstandard wrote this table in six point three megabytes, Snappy, the default, in nine point four, but Zstandard decompresses slower. Over a slow link the smaller file wins; on a fast disk, the faster codec.

part.text: Question five. What is partitioning, and what makes a good partition key? Partitioning splits a table into folders by a column's value, usually a date.

part-month.text: Here the year goes into one folder per month: twelve files. Ask for March, and DuckDB's plan scans one file of the twelve.

part-region.text: Filter on region instead, and it reads all twelve: pruning only works on the key. So a good key is the column queries filter on most, with partitions even and not too small.

part-fn.text: On many engines, a function wrapped around the key defeats pruning. DuckDB applied it to each folder's name and still read one file, so check your engine's plan.

cl.text: Question six. What is clustering, or sorting, within a partition? It orders the rows inside the files, so like values sit together.

cl-stats.text: Parquet keeps a minimum and a maximum for every column in each row group, here about a hundred twenty-three thousand rows. In date order, each group spans about six weeks, so a query for March reads only two groups of nine.

cl-shuffle.text: Shuffle the same rows, and every group spans the whole year. Nothing can be skipped, and DuckDB read five times the bytes. The minimum and maximum do the skipping, no index needed.

sm.text: Question seven. What is the tradeoff between file size and the small files problem?

sm-day.text: Partition the same year by day: three hundred sixty-six files of twenty-seven kilobytes each. Each has its own footer and must be listed and opened, so the engine spends its time on files, not data.

sm-large.text: Too large hurts too: fewer pieces to spread across workers, and coarser pruning. The usual target is about a hundred twenty-eight megabytes to a gigabyte a file.

sm-fix.text: Fix them with compaction, a job that rewrites many small files into a few large ones, or let a table format like Delta Lake or Iceberg compact them for you.

cost.text: Question eight. What drives cost in a cloud data warehouse, and how do you control it? Most bill for the data a query scans, like BigQuery, or for the compute time it uses, like Snowflake and Redshift.

cost-read.text: So read less. The revenue query read thirty-nine point two megabytes of CSV, and five of Parquet. Asked about March alone, from the monthly folders, it read four hundred twenty-three kilobytes.

cost-compute.text: Then compute less often: incremental models instead of full refreshes, stored results for heavy, repeated queries, warehouses that suspend when idle, and cold data on cheaper storage.

lake.text: Question nine. What is a data lake versus a warehouse versus a lakehouse? A warehouse stores structured, cleaned data in its own format, tuned for sequel.

lake-lake.text: A data lake keeps raw files, like Parquet and Avro, on cheap object storage: open and flexible, but with no transactions and no schema enforcement.

lake-log.text: A lakehouse puts a transaction log over those files, with a table format such as Delta Lake, Iceberg or Hudi. Each commit records which files make up the table, so every reader sees one consistent version.

lake-gives.text: That gives ACID transactions, atomic, consistent, isolated and durable, plus enforced schemas, upserts, and time travel to older versions: warehouse reliability on the lake's open, cheaper storage.

next.text: All of it assumes the data lands on time, every day. Keeping it running on time is the next round. Next: orchestration and reliability.
